Starting things.name: Starting things
Starting things.description: You lower the cost of beginning. A rough attempt from you often does more than another round of discussion, because it gives everyone something real to react to.
Starting things.action_tip: Take the first step on something your group keeps talking about, then hand it over with a clear note on what's left.
Starting things.shadow: Colleagues can feel they were overtaken before they had their say.
Starting things.overuse: You leave a trail of open beginnings that other people are expected to finish.

Finishing things.name: Finishing things
Finishing things.description: You don't count nearly done as done. You close the gaps that other people step around, so work you touch actually arrives.
Finishing things.action_tip: Offer to own the final stage of a shared project, and agree what counts as finished before you begin.
Finishing things.shadow: People who think in drafts can find your push to close things premature.
Finishing things.overuse: You finish things that should have been dropped, because stopping feels like failing.

Organising the work.name: Organising the work
Organising the work.tagline: Turns a pile of tasks into a working plan.
Organising the work.description: You see how tasks, people and dates fit together, and you rearrange them until the work flows. Groups run more calmly when you've been through the plan.
Organising the work.action_tip: Spend the first ten minutes of the next group project mapping who does what by when.
Organising the work.shadow: Your structure can feel like control to people who work best loosely.
Organising the work.overuse: You keep refining the plan when the plan is no longer what's holding things up.

Holding the standard.name: Holding the standard
Holding the standard.description: You know what good looks like and you notice when the work has drifted from it. Your refusal to wave things through raises what a group produces.
Holding the standard.action_tip: Say what good looks like at the start of a task, when people can still use it.
Holding the standard.shadow: People can hear your corrections as a verdict on them.
Holding the standard.overuse: You spend your time on improvements nobody needed, and your deadlines pay for it.

Fixing what's broken.name: Fixing what's broken
Fixing what's broken.description: Failure interests you. You trace what actually went wrong and get it working, often where others have stopped trying.
Fixing what's broken.action_tip: Volunteer for one recurring annoyance in your group, and write down the cause when you find it.
Fixing what's broken.shadow: Always pointing at what's wrong can read as pessimism.
Fixing what's broken.overuse: You keep rescuing things that should have been allowed to fail or be replaced.

Staying the course.name: Staying the course
Staying the course.tagline: Keeps going long after the excitement fades.
Staying the course.description: You can hold a goal for months or years without quick rewards. Setbacks change your method more readily than your direction.
Staying the course.action_tip: Pick the long goal that matters most and set one small weekly action you can sustain.
Staying the course.shadow: Others can read your persistence as not listening when they suggest stopping.
Staying the course.overuse: You keep investing in a goal well after the evidence says to change it.

Adjusting on the fly.name: Adjusting on the fly
Adjusting on the fly.tagline: Stays useful when the plan falls apart.
Adjusting on the fly.description: Changes that would throw other people don't throw you. You rework what you're doing on the spot and carry on, which is valuable when conditions keep moving.
Adjusting on the fly.action_tip: Offer to take the piece of a project that's most likely to change.
Adjusting on the fly.shadow: People who rely on a plan can find you hard to predict.
Adjusting on the fly.overuse: You respond so well to each change that you stop steering toward anything.

Owning the outcome.name: Owning the outcome
Owning the outcome.description: When you've taken something on, it stays yours until it's resolved, including when it goes badly. People stop checking up on you because they don't need to.
Owning the outcome.action_tip: Name the thing you're answerable for this month, and tell the person who depends on it.
Owning the outcome.shadow: Taking everything on yourself can leave others feeling they aren't trusted with any of it.
Owning the outcome.overuse: You absorb blame and workload that belong to someone else.

Testing ideas.name: Testing ideas
Testing ideas.tagline: Looks for how a claim could be wrong.
Testing ideas.description: You check whether an idea survives contact with evidence, including your own ideas. Bad plans tend to die earlier when you're in the room.
Testing ideas.action_tip: Before your next decision, write down what result would prove you wrong.
Testing ideas.shadow: Your questions can land as doubt about the person who brought the idea.
Testing ideas.overuse: You pick apart everything, and ideas stop being brought to you at all.

Connecting ideas.name: Connecting ideas
Connecting ideas.tagline: Sees links between things kept apart.
Connecting ideas.description: You collect examples from different places and notice when one solves a problem in another. New approaches often come from these unexpected joins.
Connecting ideas.action_tip: Ask how a field far from yours has dealt with the problem you're working on.
Connecting ideas.shadow: Your leaps can be hard to follow if you skip the steps in between.
Connecting ideas.overuse: You find so many links that the group loses track of the actual problem.

Looking ahead.name: Looking ahead
Looking ahead.tagline: Decides with the long run in view.
Looking ahead.description: You judge today's options by where they lead. You often prepare for changes before others have seen them coming.
Looking ahead.action_tip: Add one line to your next proposal saying what it will mean in three years.
Looking ahead.shadow: People with urgent problems can feel your long view ignores what they're dealing with now.
Looking ahead.overuse: You're so busy with what comes next that this month's work goes unattended.

Digging deep.name: Digging deep
Digging deep.description: You go to the source and stay with a subject well past what a task strictly needs. That depth lets you see what quick readers miss.
Digging deep.action_tip: Become the person who has read the source on one topic that matters to your group.
Digging deep.shadow: Others can feel lost or lectured when you give the whole answer.
Digging deep.overuse: You keep reading when the decision needed you to stop and commit.

Weighing risk.name: Weighing risk
Weighing risk.tagline: Sees the downside before it arrives.
Weighing risk.description: You think through consequences, costs and fallbacks while others are still excited. Decisions you've examined are less likely to end in expensive surprises.
Weighing risk.action_tip: Run a five-minute 'how could this fail?' check before your group commits to a plan.
Weighing risk.shadow: Your caution can look like a lack of belief in the idea.
Weighing risk.overuse: You keep weighing until the opportunity has gone, and call that being careful.

Simplifying the complex.name: Simplifying the complex
Simplifying the complex.tagline: Finds the short version that's still true.
Simplifying the complex.description: You strip problems down to what matters and say it clearly. People understand things faster after you've been through them.
Simplifying the complex.action_tip: Turn the next long document your group relies on into one page, and check it with an expert.
Simplifying the complex.shadow: People who value nuance can feel their concerns were cut.
Simplifying the complex.overuse: You simplify past the point of accuracy, and the missing detail comes back later.

Inventing options.name: Inventing options
Inventing options.tagline: Always has another way to try.
Inventing options.description: You come up with other options readily, especially when a group has decided there are only two choices. More good options means better decisions.
Inventing options.action_tip: Bring three different approaches to your next planning discussion, including one that seems odd.
Inventing options.shadow: A steady flow of new ideas can feel exhausting to people trying to execute the last one.
Inventing options.overuse: You keep opening options when the group needs you to help close one.

Learning fast.name: Learning fast
Learning fast.tagline: Becomes useful quickly in unfamiliar territory.
Learning fast.description: You enjoy being new at something and you get to working knowledge quickly. You're a good person to send into an area nobody on the team understands.
Learning fast.action_tip: Take on the part of a project that nobody knows how to do, and share what you find.
Learning fast.shadow: Your quick confidence can irritate people who've spent years in a field.
Learning fast.overuse: You move on as soon as something gets familiar, and depth never quite arrives.

Taking the lead.name: Taking the lead
Taking the lead.tagline: Steps up when nobody's in charge.
Taking the lead.description: You're willing to set a direction and ask people to follow it. Groups stuck in hesitation start moving when you take the decision on.
Taking the lead.action_tip: Next time a group stalls, propose a decision with a time limit and ask who objects.
Taking the lead.shadow: People can feel they were directed when they wanted to be consulted.
Taking the lead.overuse: You take over rooms that would have been fine without you, and others stop stepping up.

Winning support.name: Winning support
Winning support.description: You work out what people care about and frame an idea so that it connects. Proposals tend to move further when you've spoken to the right people first.
Winning support.action_tip: Before your next proposal, talk to the person most likely to oppose it and ask what would change their mind.
Winning support.shadow: Skilled persuasion can make people wonder what you really think.
Winning support.overuse: You win agreement that doesn't last, because it was your energy they agreed with.

Reading people.name: Reading people
Reading people.description: You pick up on mood, tension and what motivates each person. You often know something is wrong well before it's mentioned.
Reading people.action_tip: In your next group meeting, privately note who seems unconvinced, and ask them afterwards.
Reading people.shadow: People can feel exposed when you notice more than they meant to show.
Reading people.overuse: You act on what you've sensed without checking it, and sometimes you're wrong.

Helping others grow.name: Helping others grow
Helping others grow.description: You spot what someone could do next and invest time helping them get there. People tend to become more capable around you.
Helping others grow.action_tip: Choose one person this month and hand them something you'd normally do yourself, with support.
Helping others grow.overuse: You spend your time on other people's development and yours quietly stops.

Building trust.name: Building trust
Building trust.tagline: The person others rely on and confide in.
Building trust.description: You invest in relationships before you need them, and you behave the same whoever is in the room. Over years, that becomes a strong working network.
Building trust.action_tip: Contact someone you've worked well with, without asking them for anything.
Building trust.shadow: Newcomers can feel outside your established circle.
Building trust.overuse: Protecting a relationship stops you from saying something it needs to hear.

Easing conflict.name: Easing conflict
Easing conflict.tagline: Helps people get unstuck from each other.
Easing conflict.description: You stay calm in tense moments and find the part both sides can accept. Groups recover faster from disagreement with you around.
Easing conflict.action_tip: Next time two people talk past each other, restate each side and ask whether you got it right.
Easing conflict.shadow: People who want a fight settled can feel you're smoothing it over.
Easing conflict.overuse: You calm disagreements that needed to be had, and the real issue stays open.

Including everyone.name: Including everyone
Including everyone.description: You notice who is missing from the room or the conversation and you bring them in. Groups hear more views and lose fewer people that way.
Including everyone.action_tip: Ask the quietest person in your next meeting what they think, and give them time to answer.
Including everyone.shadow: People in a hurry can find the extra voices slow.
Including everyone.overuse: You seek so much input that nobody's sure when the decision was made.

Speaking plainly.name: Speaking plainly
Speaking plainly.tagline: Says it clearly, and out loud.
Speaking plainly.description: You can put a view into words and say it to the people concerned. Others know where they stand, and problems get named earlier.
Speaking plainly.action_tip: Say out loud the one thing your group has been avoiding, along with what you'd suggest.
Speaking plainly.shadow: Your directness can feel blunt to people who needed more care around the message.
Speaking plainly.overuse: You say it because it's true, without asking whether this is the time or the person.
